cells.tense: The work is at the bench right now and the hands know more than they did last month.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Take a part of this craft you've been handling as all one piece, and look at it closely enough to see where it divides. Don't change what you're doing yet — just find the seam.
cells.core:
You can deepen a thing without forcing it. When nothing is urgent, you still sit down with the work and a pass gets more precise than the last, and the sitting is not loneliness — it connects you to the thing itself. That's the balance: the practice flows, and the refinement serves the growing rather than your worry about it.

The way to feed it next is to make a distinction finer. Look at a part of this craft closely enough to see where it actually divides — which part matters and which was only ever noise. You don't have to do anything with what you find. Seeing the seam is the whole move this time, and it sharpens the eye you'll use on everything after.
cells.sheetLine: You can go deeper without pushing, and that's the skill itself.
cells.verb: deepening a craft past the point where it stops being new
cells.place: where something small is being tended toward what it's becoming

cells.tense: The next stages of the work are being built before this one has been finished.
cells.act: mark the good thing together, out loud
cells.ask: When something in this craft goes well, take it to the people around it and say the good of it out loud, where they can hear you — not a status update, just the good news.
cells.core:
Caring for what's growing has tipped into running ahead of it. The whole arc gets planned before the thing has grown into its next size, and the care starts to feel like pressure the work didn't ask for. You keep checking the far end to make sure it will hold. It will hold better if you let it arrive.

What the balance needs is to be shared, not managed. When something finally goes well, take it to the people who are near it and say so out loud, together. Let the gladness land where they can hear it instead of logging it and moving to the next stage. Joy said out loud is how a craft stops being a private worry and becomes something others can stand in with you.
cells.sheetLine: You keep bracing for stages the work hasn't reached yet.
cells.verb: deepening a craft past the point where it stops being new
cells.place: where something small is being tended toward what it's becoming

cells.tense: The craft has been sitting untouched while the person waits for a sign that it is worth doing.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Before anyone asks what you're making or why, say it out loud once: what it is, what it's for, how it goes. Don't wait to be sure — one clear sentence to whoever's there.
cells.core:
The work sits untouched and you haven't been picking it up. You hover at the edge of starting until something tells you it's allowed — a sign, permission, certainty that the thing deserves the time. Hovering is the whole stance now, and the craft you could be deepening is exactly as far along as it was when you left it.

You get moving again by saying out loud what you're making before you're sure of it. One plain sentence to whoever's there about what it is and what it's for. The frame gets declared first and trusted afterward, and declaring it is how the energy comes back to a practice that's been standing at a threshold already crossed.
cells.sheetLine: You're still waiting for permission to begin something you already started.
cells.verb: deepening a craft past the point where it stops being new
cells.place: where something small is being tended toward what it's becoming

cells.tense: The effort that is holding someone else's thing together is not being counted as theirs.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Take the next piece at a pace you could hold for a month, not a week — and where you've been going faster to prop something up, ease off to that slower pace on purpose, where whoever's watching can see.
cells.core:
Your telling has you as the one who was around while something else grew. But the reliable ground other people lean on in this is yours — you worked at the bench and held it steady through the parts nobody saw. The credit for the craftsmanship has been left with whoever happened to be nearby, and you've gone along with the story that it kept itself standing.

What returns it is moving at a pace your own feeling can carry. Take the next piece at a speed you could hold for a month rather than a day, and where you've been moving faster to hold something up, set it down to that slower pace on purpose, where it can be seen. Steady momentum, kept where they can watch it, is the version of this that finally has your name on it.
cells.sheetLine: You carried it and you'd say it just held.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person has actually reached the threshold of real mastery in this practice — the record says the transient marks a threshold being approached, and I've written the Too Much and Unacknowledged cells as if the skill is already load-bearing for other people. A reader could reasonably say the craft is new or the people standing on it are three rather than thirty. The asks survive that: sorting what matters, marking a good thing out loud, putting the frame on the table, and moving at a sustainable pace are all useful whether or not mastery has arrived. The sentence that serves me more than them is the Too Much image about stacks growing in the dark — it's a better line than it is a description, so I've kept the camera on one concrete move instead.
